pos: n. (the edge of a road; the place of watching, of ambush, and in the parable the trodden ground where seed cannot enter)
etymology: From way and side. The Authorized Version prints it as one word in 1 Samuel and the Psalms, and as two — way side — in the parable of the sower; the ground is the same, the hard-packed edge of a path.
biblical_def: The wayside is where a man sits to watch for news he dreads. “And when he came, lo, Eli sat upon a seat by the wayside watching: for his heart trembled for the ark of God” (1 Samuel 4:13). It is also where enemies work: “The proud have hid a snare for me, and cords; they have spread a net by the wayside; they have set gins for me” (Psalm 140:5). The most familiar use is the first soil of the parable: “And when he sowed, some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up” (Matthew 13:4). The Lord interprets it Himself, and the interpretation turns on the ground's hardness: “When any one heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart. This is he which received seed by the way side” (Matthew 13:19). The path is not barren for lack of seed or sun; it is barren because it has been walked on until nothing can get in. The seed lies exposed on the surface, and the birds take what never went down. Wayside ground is made, not born — every foot that crosses a field packs it a little harder.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines way-side as the side of the way, the border of a road, and way as a passage, road or street.
webster_full: WAY-SIDE, n. The side of the way; the border of a road.
WAY, n. Literally, a passing; hence, a passage; the place of passing; a road; a highway; a street.
SNARE, n. An instrument for catching animals, particularly birds, by the leg.
2. Any thing by which one is entangled and brought into trouble.
GIN, n. A trap; a snare.
scriptures: Matthew 13:4
And when he sowed, some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up:
Matthew 13:19
When any one heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart. This is he which received seed by the way side.
1 Samuel 4:13
And when he came, lo, Eli sat upon a seat by the wayside watching: for his heart trembled for the ark of God. And when the man came into the city, and told it, all the city cried out.
Psalm 140:5
The proud have hid a snare for me, and cords; they have spread a net by the wayside; they have set gins for me. Selah.
corruption_summary: Wayside hearing is treated as a fixed type of person rather than a condition of ground that traffic produced and grace can break up.
corruption_paragraphs: The four soils are often preached as four kinds of people, sorted permanently, so that the wayside hearer is simply a reprobate and the matter ends there. The figure itself resists that. A path is hard because it has been walked on; it was field once. Jeremiah and Hosea both command what follows from this — break up your fallow ground — and the ploughman's answer to a beaten track is not to declare it a different substance but to break it open. The doctrine of election is not touched by saying so; God is the one who gives the new heart, and the means He uses include the plough of the law and the preaching that turns the surface over.

The second and more searching application is that hardness is produced by traffic, and traffic is the ordinary condition of a modern life. The wayside hearer in Matthew 13:19 is not hostile; he simply understandeth it not, and the wicked one takes the seed before it can sink. That is an exact portrait of hearing a sermon while the mind is already elsewhere. Eli sat by the wayside because his heart trembled for the ark of God, and even his watching was too late to change what he had failed to correct in his sons. A church that fills every hour and leaves no ground unwalked should not be surprised when the seed lies on the surface.
roots_summary: Greek hodos (G3598), a way or road — Matthew 13:4, 13:19; Hebrew derek and yad derek, the hand or side of the way — 1 Samuel 4:13, Psalm 140:5.
roots_lines: Greek para ten hodon — beside the way; Matthew 13:4, Mark 4:4, Luke 8:5, the first of the four soils.
Greek harpazo (G726) — to snatch away by force; Matthew 13:19, of the wicked one taking the seed.
Hebrew derek — a way, road, journey; the common word behind the Old Testament uses.
Hebrew moqesh — a snare, a gin; Psalm 140:5, set by the wayside where men must pass.
Hosea 10:12 supplies the answer to hard ground: break up your fallow ground, for it is time to seek the LORD.
usage: “Some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them” — nothing went down.
“Eli sat upon a seat by the wayside watching” — the place of dreaded news.
A path is hard because it was walked on; it was field once.

pos: adj. and adv. (thirty times over; the least of the three yields from good ground in the parable of the sower)
etymology: From thirty and the suffix -fold (Old English -feald, a folding or multiplying). The Greek is simply triakonta, thirty, with the sense of increase supplied by the context of sowing.
biblical_def: “But other fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold” (Matthew 13:8). Mark reverses the order and so puts thirty first: “And these are they which are sown on good ground; such as hear the word, and receive it, and bring forth fruit, some thirtyfold, some sixty, and some an hundred” (Mark 4:20). The interpretation names what makes ground good: “he that received seed into the good ground is he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit” (Matthew 13:23). Three observations follow from the numbers. First, all three yields are the good ground — thirtyfold is not a partial success but a genuine harvest, and the sower is not disappointed with it. Second, the differences are real; Scripture does not flatten believers into uniformity, and no reason for the difference is offered. Third, even thirty is an extraordinary return by any ancient standard of agriculture, so the least of the three is already an abundance. The parable measures a hearer by whether he bears fruit at all, not by how his crop compares with his neighbour's.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fold as a term denoting multiplication or repetition of a quantity, as in twofold or tenfold.
webster_full: FOLD, a termination denoting a certain number or quantity added, as in twofold, tenfold, that is, twice, ten times.
HUNDREDFOLD, n. A hundred times as much.
YIELD, v.i. To produce, as land, stock or capital; to bring in as revenue or profit.
INCREASE, n. Augmentation; a growing larger; produce; profit.
GOOD GROUND, land fit for tillage; that which produces a crop.
scriptures: Matthew 13:8
But other fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold.
Mark 4:20
And these are they which are sown on good ground; such as hear the word, and receive it, and bring forth fruit, some thirtyfold, some sixty, and some an hundred.
Matthew 13:23
But he that received seed into the good ground is he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit, and bringeth forth, some an hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.
Matthew 13:19
When any one heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart. This is he which received seed by the way side.
corruption_summary: The three yields are turned into a ranking of Christians, so that thirtyfold believers are treated as second-class and driven to imitate a hundredfold.
corruption_paragraphs: A common misuse of this parable turns the numbers into tiers of discipleship, with sermons urging hearers to move from thirty to a hundred as though the yield were a matter of resolve. The text assigns no cause for the difference and issues no exhortation about it. All three are good ground, all three bear fruit, and the contrast the Lord draws is not between thirty and a hundred but between fruit and no fruit at all. Turning the parable into a scale of attainment produces exactly what Scripture forbids elsewhere — believers measuring themselves by one another, which Paul says is not wise.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that fruitfulness is the evidence of life, not the price of it. The good ground does not produce in order to become good ground; it produces because it is. The Confession states the corresponding doctrine plainly: good works are the fruits and evidences of a true and lively faith, not the cause of salvation. A congregation taught to strive for a hundredfold as a condition of acceptance will be either proud or despairing, and both conditions are cured by noticing that the parable's good ground is defined by hearing and understanding the word — which is itself a gift.
roots_summary: Greek triakonta (G5144), thirty — Matthew 13:8, 13:23, Mark 4:8, 4:20; set with hexekonta (G1835), sixty, and hekaton (G1540), a hundred.
roots_lines: Greek triakonta (G5144) — thirty; in the parable at Matthew 13:8, 13:23, Mark 4:8 and Mark 4:20.
Greek kalos (G2570) — good, fine; the good ground of Matthew 13:8, a word of quality rather than mere usefulness.
Greek karpophoreo (G2592) — to bear fruit; Mark 4:20, and the test the parable actually applies.
Greek suniemi (G4920) — to understand, to put together; Matthew 13:23, what distinguishes good ground from the wayside.
Luke 8:15 adds the note the other accounts omit: an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience.
usage: “Some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold” — all three are the good ground.
“Hear the word, and receive it, and bring forth fruit” — the test is fruit, not its size.
Thirty was an extraordinary return; the least of the three is already abundance.

pos: n. (a reaper; in Isaiah and Jeremiah, a figure of judgment gathering a nation as a man gathers corn)
etymology: From harvest (Old English haerfest, autumn) and man. It renders the Hebrew qatsir in a construction meaning the one who reaps, and both occurrences stand in oracles of judgment.
biblical_def: Isaiah pictures the stripping of Israel: “And it shall be as when the harvestman gathereth the corn, and reapeth the ears with his arm; and it shall be as he that gathereth ears in the valley of Rephaim” (Isaiah 17:5). The comparison is grim — a nation taken as cleanly as a reaper takes a field — and yet the very next verse holds the mercy that always accompanies Isaiah's judgments: “Yet gleaning grapes shall be left in it, as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three berries in the top of the uppermost bough” (Isaiah 17:6). The reaper is thorough; the remnant survives anyway. Jeremiah uses the same figure and withholds even the gleaning: “Even the carcases of men shall fall as dung upon the open field, and as the handful after the harvestman, and none shall gather them” (Jeremiah 9:22). The handful dropped behind a reaper is exactly what the law commanded to be left for the poor; here there is no one to gather it. Joel completes the picture with the summons: “Put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe: come, get you down; for the press is full, the fats overflow; for their wickedness is great” (Joel 3:13). Harvest in the prophets is not merely ingathering. It is the moment a crop has finished growing and the time for cutting has come.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines harvest as the season of reaping and gathering in corn, the ripe corn collected, and figuratively the product of labour or the fruit of one's conduct.
webster_full: HARVEST, n. The season of reaping and gathering in corn or other crops.
2. The ripe corn or grain collected and secured in barns or stacks.
3. The product of labor; fruit or fruits.
4. Fruit or fruits; effects; consequences; as, the harvest of sin.
REAP, v.t. To cut grain with a sickle; as, to reap wheat or rye.
scriptures: Isaiah 17:5
And it shall be as when the harvestman gathereth the corn, and reapeth the ears with his arm; and it shall be as he that gathereth ears in the valley of Rephaim.
Jeremiah 9:22
Speak, Thus saith the LORD, Even the carcases of men shall fall as dung upon the open field, and as the handful after the harvestman, and none shall gather them.
Isaiah 17:6

Yet gleaning grapes shall be left in it, as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three berries in the top of the uppermost bough, four or five in the outmost fruitful branches thereof, saith the LORD God of Israel.
Joel 3:13
Put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe: come, get you down; for the press is full, the fats overflow; for their wickedness is great.
corruption_summary: Harvest language is used almost exclusively for evangelistic success, and its far commoner prophetic sense — judgment on a ripened wickedness — is left unpreached.
corruption_paragraphs: Ask most congregations what harvest means in Scripture and the answer will be missions: the fields white already to harvest, the labourers few. That use is genuine and the Lord Himself made it. But the dominant prophetic use is the other one, and it is not gentle — Joel's sickle is put in for their wickedness is great, and Revelation 14 takes up Joel's image for the winepress of the wrath of God. Harvest in the prophets marks the point at which a thing has finished growing. That is why the parable of the wheat and tares lets both grow together until the harvest: judgment is delayed not because sin is tolerated but because the crop is not yet ripe.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the mercy that Isaiah writes into the middle of the judgment. The harvestman strips the field, and two or three berries remain in the top of the uppermost bough. The doctrine of the remnant is one of the most persistent in the Old Testament and one of the most neglected in preaching about national decline, where the choice is usually presented as revival or ruin. Isaiah offers a third possibility and it is the one that has usually happened: the field is cut, and God keeps a seed. The gleanings left after the reaper were the poor man's portion by law, and they are the shape of God's mercy in judgment.
roots_summary: Hebrew qatsir, harvest or reaping — Isaiah 17:5, Jeremiah 9:22; amir, a swath or handful — Jeremiah 9:22; maggal, a sickle — Joel 3:13.
roots_lines: Hebrew qatsir — harvest, the reaping and the crop reaped; the root behind harvestman in both occurrences.
Hebrew amir — a swath, the handful left behind the reaper; Jeremiah 9:22, and the poor man's portion under Leviticus 19:9.
Hebrew maggal — a sickle; Joel 3:13, and Jeremiah 50:16.
Hebrew Rephaim — the valley south-west of Jerusalem, proverbially fertile; Isaiah 17:5.
Isaiah 17:6 supplies the counterweight: gleaning grapes shall be left in it — the remnant doctrine in a figure.
usage: “As when the harvestman gathereth the corn” — a nation taken as cleanly as a field.
“Put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe” — ripeness, not merely ingathering.
“Yet gleaning grapes shall be left in it” — the remnant survives the reaper.

pos: n. (the gathering in of the year's produce; the name of the third of Israel's annual feasts, kept at the year's end)
etymology: From in and gather, rendering Hebrew asiph, an ingathering, from asaph, to gather. It names the same festival called elsewhere the feast of tabernacles or booths.
biblical_def: “And the feast of harvest, the firstfruits of thy labours, which thou hast sown in the field: and the feast of ingathering, which is in the end of the year, when thou hast gathered in thy labours out of the field” (Exodus 23:16). It is the last of the three pilgrim feasts, and the command is repeated at the renewal of the covenant: “And thou shalt observe the feast of weeks, of the firstfruits of wheat harvest, and the feast of ingathering at the year's end” (Exodus 34:22). Leviticus gives the manner: “Also in the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when ye have gathered in the fruit of the land, ye shall keep a feast unto the LORD seven days” (Leviticus 23:39). Two things mark the feast. It comes after everything is in, so it is a festival of completed provision rather than of hope; and it was kept in booths, so that a people sitting on a full year's harvest spent the week in temporary shelters remembering that their fathers had none. Prosperity and pilgrimage were deliberately held together. The prophets take up the same figure for the last gathering of all, when the nations come to keep the feast (Zechariah 14), and the New Testament fills it out with a harvest at the end of the world.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ingathering as the act of collecting and securing the fruits of the earth, and the harvest.
webster_full: INGATHERING, n. The act of collecting and securing the fruits of the earth; harvest.
GATHER, v.t. To bring together; to collect a number of separate things.
2. To get in harvest; to reap or cut and bring into barns or stores.
TABERNACLE, n. A tent; a temporary habitation.
BOOTH, n. A house or shed built of boards, boughs of trees or other slight materials, for a temporary residence.
scriptures: Exodus 23:16

And the feast of harvest, the firstfruits of thy labours, which thou hast sown in the field: and the feast of ingathering, which is in the end of the year, when thou hast gathered in thy labours out of the field.
Exodus 34:22
And thou shalt observe the feast of weeks, of the firstfruits of wheat harvest, and the feast of ingathering at the year's end.
Leviticus 23:39

Also in the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when ye have gathered in the fruit of the land, ye shall keep a feast unto the LORD seven days: on the first day shall be a sabbath, and on the eighth day shall be a sabbath.
Joel 3:13
Put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe: come, get you down; for the press is full, the fats overflow; for their wickedness is great.
corruption_summary: Thanksgiving for provision is separated from the remembrance of dependence, and a feast designed to unsettle the prosperous becomes a celebration of having arrived.
corruption_paragraphs: The genius of the feast of ingathering is its timing and its housing. It falls when the barns are full, and it requires the people to leave their houses and live in booths for a week. A nation at its most self-sufficient moment was commanded to sit in a shelter that would not survive a storm, and to remember that the LORD made Israel dwell in booths when He brought them out of Egypt. Harvest festivals detached from that discipline become simple congratulation, and a church that gives thanks for its provision without any reminder of its dependence has kept the feast of harvest and dropped the booths.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordering of the whole calendar. Israel's year was structured by three appearances before the LORD, and the shape of the year taught the doctrine: firstfruits at the beginning, weeks in the middle, ingathering at the end. Time itself was catechetical. Where the Christian year has been reduced to two heavily commercialised days, the church has lost an instrument God evidently thought worth commanding, and gained nothing in its place. The Lord's Day remains, and it is the one ordinance of time He has appointed for the church — which makes its erosion a graver loss than is usually reckoned.
roots_summary: Hebrew asiph, ingathering — Exodus 23:16, 34:22; from asaph, to gather; the same feast called sukkoth, booths, in Leviticus 23:34.
roots_lines: Hebrew asiph — an ingathering; Exodus 23:16 and Exodus 34:22, the name of the third pilgrim feast.
Hebrew asaph — to gather, to take in; the root, used also of being gathered to one's people in death.
Hebrew sukkoth — booths; Leviticus 23:34, the same feast named from the shelters it required.
Hebrew chag — a pilgrim feast; the three appearances of Exodus 23:14-17.
Leviticus 23:43 gives the reason for the booths: that your generations may know that I made the children of Israel to dwell in booths.
usage: “The feast of ingathering, which is in the end of the year” — kept after everything is in.
“When ye have gathered in the fruit of the land, ye shall keep a feast unto the LORD” — provision and pilgrimage together.
A people with full barns spent the week in booths.

pos: n. pl. (those who harvest a vineyard; in the prophets, a figure for a judgment that nevertheless leaves gleanings, unlike a thief)
etymology: A compound of grape (Old French grape, a bunch) and gatherer, rendering Hebrew botsrim, from batsar, to cut off or gather grapes — the vintagers.
biblical_def: The word occurs in two oracles that share a single argument. Jeremiah, against Edom: “If grapegatherers come to thee, would they not leave some gleaning grapes? if thieves by night, they will destroy till they have enough” (Jeremiah 49:9). Obadiah, against the same nation: “If thieves came to thee, if robbers by night, (how art thou cut off!) would they not have stolen till they had enough? if the grapegatherers came to thee, would they not leave some grapes?” (Obadiah 1:5). The reasoning runs by contrast. A vintager works under the law that forbids stripping a vineyard bare, so something is always left for the poor and the stranger; a thief takes only what he wants and leaves the rest. Either way, something remains. What is coming on Edom will be worse than both: “But I have made Esau bare, I have uncovered his secret places, and he shall not be able to hide himself” (Jeremiah 49:10). Nothing left at all. Micah uses the same picture for his own grief at a nation with no righteous man in it: “Woe is me! for I am as when they have gathered the summer fruits, as the grapegleanings of the vintage: there is no cluster to eat” (Micah 7:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a gatherer as one who collects, and vintage as the produce of the vine for the year, the time of gathering grapes.
webster_full: GATHERER, n. One who gathers or collects.
VINTAGE, n. The produce of the vine for the season, in grapes or in wine.
2. The time of gathering the crop of grapes.
GLEAN, v.t. To gather the stalks and ears of grain which reapers leave behind them.
VINEYARD, n. A plantation of vines producing grapes.
scriptures: Jeremiah 49:9
If grapegatherers come to thee, would they not leave some gleaning grapes? if thieves by night, they will destroy till they have enough.
Obadiah 1:5
If thieves came to thee, if robbers by night, (how art thou cut off!) would they not have stolen till they had enough? if the grapegatherers came to thee, would they not leave some grapes?
Jeremiah 49:10
But I have made Esau bare, I have uncovered his secret places, and he shall not be able to hide himself: his seed is spoiled, and his brethren, and his neighbours, and he is not.
Micah 7:1
Woe is me! for I am as when they have gathered the summer fruits, as the grapegleanings of the vintage: there is no cluster to eat: my soul desired the firstripe fruit.
corruption_summary: The gleaning law behind the figure is read as an antique charity provision, when it is a limit God imposed on the rights of an owner over his own field.
corruption_paragraphs: The whole force of Jeremiah 49:9 depends on a law the modern reader has to be told about. Leviticus 19:10 forbids gleaning a vineyard bare or gathering the fallen grapes; they are to be left for the poor and the stranger. That is why a vintager is a lower bar than a thief in the prophet's argument: even a legitimate harvester is under a restriction. The law asserts something the current debate over property rarely allows to be said — that ownership is real and is not absolute, because the owner is himself a tenant under God. Neither of the standard modern positions holds that: one treats property as absolute, the other abolishes it. Scripture does neither, and leaves the corners of the field standing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word. The principle to recover is the dignity of the arrangement. The gleaning law does not transfer the harvest; it leaves it in the field, so that the poor gather it with their own hands and are fed by work rather than by handout. Ruth is the extended illustration, and Boaz's charge to his young men to let fall some handfuls of purpose is the law kept generously. That pattern — provision the poor must still labour to take up, arranged so that no one is humiliated in receiving it — is a wiser design than most of what has replaced it, and it came from the same statute book that told the vintager to leave some grapes.
roots_summary: Hebrew botsrim, grape-gatherers — Jeremiah 49:9, Obadiah 5; from batsar, to cut off or gather grapes; oleloth, gleaning grapes — Jeremiah 49:9, Micah 7:1.
roots_lines: Hebrew batsar — to cut off, to gather grapes; the root of botsrim, the vintagers.
Hebrew oleloth — the gleanings of a vineyard, what the vintager must leave; Jeremiah 49:9, Micah 7:1, Isaiah 17:6.
Hebrew Esau and Edom — the nation both oracles address, kin to Israel and hostile to her.
Leviticus 19:10 is the law the figure presupposes: thou shalt not glean thy vineyard, neither shalt thou gather every grape.
Ruth 2:16 shows the law kept with generosity: let fall also some of the handfuls of purpose for her.
usage: “Would they not leave some gleaning grapes?” — even the harvester is under a limit.
“I have made Esau bare” — less left than a thief would leave.
The corners of the field were never the owner's to take.

pos: adv. (abundantly, in full measure; used of a rich man's ground, of God's recompense, and of counsel fully declared)
etymology: From plenty, Latin plenus, full. The Authorized Version uses it for several Hebrew and Greek constructions where the sense is simply in abundance.
biblical_def: The most famous use opens a parable: “And he spake a parable unto them, saying, The ground of a certain rich man brought forth plentifully” (Luke 12:16). The abundance is not the man's sin — the ground brought it forth, which is to say God gave it. His sin appears in what he does next: he pulls down his barns to build greater, and speaks to his own soul about many years. God's answer names him: “Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?” (Luke 12:20). The Psalmist uses the word of God's dealing: “O love the LORD, all ye his saints: for the LORD preserveth the faithful, and plentifully rewardeth the proud doer” (Psalm 31:23). The abundance there falls on both sides of the ledger — preservation for the faithful, and a full measure of recompense for the proud. Job uses it with heavy irony against his comforters: “How hast thou counselled him that hath no wisdom? and how hast thou plentifully declared the thing as it is?” (Job 26:3). Abundance in Scripture is never neutral; everything depends on whose it is and what is done with it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines plentifully as copiously, abundantly, with an ample supply.
webster_full: PLENTIFULLY, adv. Copiously; abundantly; with ample supply.
PLENTIFUL, a. Existing in great plenty; abundant; copious.
2. Yielding abundant crops; fruitful; as a plentiful year.
PLENTY, n. Abundance; copiousness; full or adequate supply.
BARN, n. A covered building for securing grain, hay, flax, and other productions of the earth.
scriptures: Luke 12:16
And he spake a parable unto them, saying, The ground of a certain rich man brought forth plentifully:
Luke 12:20
But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?
Psalm 31:23
O love the LORD, all ye his saints: for the LORD preserveth the faithful, and plentifully rewardeth the proud doer.
Job 26:3
How hast thou counselled him that hath no wisdom? and how hast thou plentifully declared the thing as it is?
corruption_summary: Abundance is taken as a verdict — proof of God's approval, or proof of guilt — and the parable makes it neither.
corruption_paragraphs: Prosperity teaching reads a plentiful harvest as evidence of favour, and Luke 12:16 begins exactly where that doctrine would like it to: the ground of a certain rich man brought forth plentifully. Two verses later God calls him a fool. The abundance was genuine and it was given, and it settled nothing about the man's standing. What condemned him was the soliloquy — my fruits, my barns, my goods, my soul — and the assumption of many years. The parable ends with the principle: so is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God. Wealth is a stewardship whose accounting can be called in tonight.

The mirror error treats plenty as guilt and makes poverty a spiritual attainment, which the same Scriptures refuse. God gave the increase in the parable; the ground brought it forth; and Psalm 31:23 shows Him plentifully preserving the faithful. The Bible's consistent position is neither prosperity nor asceticism but stewardship, held with the awareness that the steward is mortal. The rich fool's real miscalculation was not that he saved but that he assumed time. This night thy soul shall be required of thee is the sentence that undoes every plan built on an unpromised tomorrow.
roots_summary: Greek euphoreo (G2164), to bear well — Luke 12:16, its only occurrence; Hebrew al yether, in abundance — Psalm 31:23; larob, in plenty — Job 26:3.
roots_lines: Greek euphoreo (G2164) — to bring forth well, to be fruitful; Luke 12:16, its only occurrence in the New Testament.
Greek aphron (G878) — senseless, a fool; Luke 12:20, God's own name for the man.
Hebrew yether — abundance, that which remains over; Psalm 31:23, of the recompense to the proud doer.
Hebrew rob — multitude, abundance; Job 26:3, in Job's ironical thanks for plentiful counsel.
Luke 12:21 states the moral: so is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.
usage: “The ground of a certain rich man brought forth plentifully” — and God called him a fool two verses later.
“Plentifully rewardeth the proud doer” — abundance falls on both sides of the ledger.
The rich fool's error was not saving; it was assuming time.

pos: n. (income, yield, return; used of a king's taxes, a nation's trade, the wicked man's gain, and wisdom's own produce)
etymology: French revenu, that which comes back, from Latin revenire, to return. The Authorized Version uses it for Hebrew tebuah (produce, increase) and for the Aramaic term for royal tax income in Ezra.
biblical_def: The word covers both public finance and personal gain, and Scripture judges the two by the same standard. The enemies of the rebuilding warn Artaxerxes that a restored Jerusalem “will they not pay toll, tribute, and custom, and so thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings” (Ezra 4:13) — an appeal to the treasury, and it worked. Tyre's commercial greatness is described the same way: “the harvest of the river, is her revenue; and she is a mart of nations” (Isaiah 23:3). Proverbs then applies the measure. Wisdom says, “My fruit is better than gold, yea, than fine gold; and my revenue than choice silver” (Proverbs 8:19) — wisdom has a yield, and it outperforms metal. Against that stands the wicked man's balance sheet: “In the house of the righteous is much treasure: but in the revenues of the wicked is trouble” (Proverbs 15:6), and the verdict that decides the whole matter: “Better is a little with righteousness than great revenues without right” (Proverbs 16:8). The Bible is not indifferent to income. It insists that the figure at the bottom is not the only figure, and that revenue gained without right is a loss recorded as a gain.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines revenue as the income of a nation or of an individual, the annual rents, profits, interest or issues of any species of property.
webster_full: REVENUE, n. In a general sense, the annual rents, profits, interest or issues of any species of property, real or personal, belonging to an individual or to the public.
2. The annual produce of taxes, excise, customs, duties, rents, &c. which a nation or state collects and receives into the treasury for public use.
3. Return; reception.
INCREASE, n. Produce, as of land; profit.
CUSTOM, n. Tribute, toll or tax paid to the sovereign for goods imported or exported.
scriptures: Proverbs 8:19
My fruit is better than gold, yea, than fine gold; and my revenue than choice silver.
Proverbs 16:8
Better is a little with righteousness than great revenues without right.
Proverbs 15:6
In the house of the righteous is much treasure: but in the revenues of the wicked is trouble.
Ezra 4:13
Be it known now unto the king, that, if this city be builded, and the walls set up again, then will they not pay toll, tribute, and custom, and so thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings.
corruption_summary: Income is treated as a number that settles the question by itself, and Proverbs insists on a second column the ledger has no place for.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 16:8 is one of the most economically subversive sentences in Scripture: better is a little with righteousness than great revenues without right. It does not say the little is more virtuous and the great more comfortable; it says the little is better, which is a claim about the actual value of the two holdings. No accounting method can express that. Every measure a business or a state uses records the great revenues as the superior position, and Scripture flatly denies it. This is not a complaint against profit — the same book praises the diligent hand and the wise woman who considereth a field and buyeth it — but a denial that the figure at the bottom is the final word.

Ezra 4:13 records how effective the appeal to revenue is against the work of God, and the tactic has not aged. The enemies of the rebuilding did not argue theology with Artaxerxes; they told him the project would cost him money, and the work stopped for years. Ministries and congregations are still halted this way, by arguments framed entirely in terms of cost and benefit where the question is actually one of obedience. Proverbs 8:19 supplies the counter-claim that must be made in reply: wisdom has a revenue of its own, and it is better than choice silver.
roots_summary: Hebrew tebuah, produce or increase — Proverbs 8:19, 15:6, 16:8; Aramaic appthom, royal revenue — Ezra 4:13.
roots_lines: Hebrew tebuah — produce, increase, revenue; Proverbs 8:19, 15:6, 16:8, and used of the yield of the land.
Aramaic term rendered revenue of the kings — Ezra 4:13, in the letter that stopped the rebuilding.
Hebrew mishpat — judgment, right; Proverbs 16:8, great revenues without right.
Hebrew chokmah — wisdom; the speaker of Proverbs 8:19, whose revenue is better than choice silver.
Proverbs 15:6 puts the two houses side by side: much treasure in one, trouble in the revenues of the other.
usage: “Better is a little with righteousness than great revenues without right” — a claim about value, not comfort.
“My revenue than choice silver” — wisdom yields, and outperforms metal.
“Thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings” — and the work of God stopped for years.

pos: n. (advancement in rank or honour; in Scripture always traced to God's hand rather than to man's striving)
etymology: Latin promovere, to move forward. The Hebrew in Psalm 75 is rum, to lift up or exalt; in Proverbs 3:35 the noun is used ironically of what fools actually receive.
biblical_def: “For promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south” (Psalm 75:6). The sentence is famous for the direction it omits. Three points of the compass are ruled out and the fourth is not named, because the answer is not a direction at all but a Person, supplied in the next verse: “But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another” (Psalm 75:7). Advancement is judicial, an act of the Judge, and He both raises and lowers. Proverbs turns the word with heavy irony: “The wise shall inherit glory: but shame shall be the promotion of fools” (Proverbs 3:35). The fool is promoted — he rises, he becomes conspicuous — and what he is elevated into is shame. The proper way to seek advancement is given in the same book, and the agent is wisdom rather than the man: “Exalt her, and she shall promote thee: she shall bring thee to honour, when thou dost embrace her” (Proverbs 4:8). A man exalts wisdom and wisdom promotes him. The order is never reversed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines promotion as advancement in station or honor, preferment, and exaltation in rank or dignity.
webster_full: PROMOTION, n. The act of promoting; advancement; preferment in rank or honor.
2. Exaltation in honor or dignity, or in rank.
PROMOTE, v.t. To forward; to advance; to contribute to the growth, enlargement or excellence of any thing.
2. To exalt; to elevate; to raise; as, to promote an officer.
PREFERMENT, n. Advancement to a higher office or dignity.
scriptures: Psalm 75:6
For promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south.
Psalm 75:7
But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another.
Proverbs 3:35
The wise shall inherit glory: but shame shall be the promotion of fools.
Proverbs 4:8
Exalt her, and she shall promote thee: she shall bring thee to honour, when thou dost embrace her.
corruption_summary: Advancement is treated as a thing to be engineered, and Psalm 75 says the compass has no direction that supplies it.
corruption_paragraphs: The whole apparatus of self-advancement — the personal brand, the positioning, the network worked with an eye to what it can yield — assumes that promotion comes from somewhere on the map. Psalm 75:6 rules out three directions and leaves the fourth unspoken because the answer is above. This is not an argument for passivity; Scripture commends diligence and says that a man diligent in his business shall stand before kings. It is a denial that the outcome is in the striver's hands. Joseph in prison, David keeping sheep, and Daniel refusing the king's meat were all promoted, and not one of them arranged it.

Proverbs 3:35 supplies the sharpest warning, and it applies inside the church as much as outside. Shame shall be the promotion of fools — the fool is genuinely elevated, and elevation is precisely his punishment, because it puts his folly where everyone can see it. Ministries have watched this happen: a man is advanced beyond his character, and the promotion does not correct the deficiency but publishes it. That is one reason the New Testament requires an elder to be proved first, and forbids a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil.
roots_summary: Hebrew rum, to be high, to exalt — Psalm 75:6-7; ruwm in the causative of God setting up and putting down; Proverbs 3:35 and 4:8 use the honour-vocabulary of the wisdom books.
roots_lines: Hebrew rum — to lift up, to exalt; Psalm 75:6-7, both of the promotion sought and the God who grants it.
Hebrew shaphel — to bring low; the counterpart in Psalm 75:7, he putteth down one and setteth up another.
Hebrew qalon — shame, dishonour; Proverbs 3:35, the promotion the fool actually receives.
Hebrew salal — to exalt, to lift up as a highway; Proverbs 4:8, exalt her and she shall promote thee.
1 Timothy 3:6 gives the New Testament caution: not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil.
usage: “Promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south” — and the fourth direction is a Person.
“Shame shall be the promotion of fools” — the elevation is itself the punishment.
“Exalt her, and she shall promote thee” — the order is never reversed.

pos: v. (past participle of shear; of sheep cut for their fleece, of a head shaved under a vow, and of a woman's covering in 1 Corinthians)
etymology: Past participle of shear, Old English sceran, to cut. The Greek in 1 Corinthians 11 is keiro, to crop or cut the hair, distinguished there from xurao, to shave with a razor.
biblical_def: The plainest use is pastoral and admiring: “Thy teeth are like a flock of sheep that are even shorn, which came up from the washing; whereof every one bear twins, and none is barren among them” (Song of Solomon 4:2) — a shorn flock coming up white from the wash. The second use is a vow: Paul, at Cenchrea, “having shorn his head… for he had a vow” (Acts 18:18), and later at Jerusalem he pays the charges of four men that they may shave their heads (Acts 21:24). The third is Paul's argument about the head covering: “For if the woman be not covered, let her also be shorn: but if it be a shame for a woman to be shorn or shaven, let her be covered” (1 Corinthians 11:6). The reasoning is by consistency. He has said that a woman praying or prophesying uncovered dishonours her head, “for that is even all one as if she were shaven” (1 Corinthians 11:5), and now presses the point: if the covering is indifferent, then be consistent and be shorn — and if that is a shame, then the covering is not indifferent either. The argument is grounded in the creational order of headship set out in the verses before it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives shorn as the participle of shear, and shear as to cut or clip with shears, especially to clip the fleece from sheep.
webster_full: SHORN, pp. of shear. Cut off; as a fleece shorn.
2. Having the hair or wool cut off or sheared.
SHEAR, v.t. To cut or clip something from the surface with an instrument of two blades; to separate the fleece from a sheep.
FLEECE, n. The coat of wool that covers a sheep or is shorn from it at one time.
VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 11:6
For if the woman be not covered, let her also be shorn: but if it be a shame for a woman to be shorn or shaven, let her be covered.
1 Corinthians 11:5
But every woman that prayeth or prophesieth with her head uncovered dishonoureth her head: for that is even all one as if she were shaven.
Acts 18:18

And Paul after this tarried there yet a good while, and then took his leave of the brethren, and sailed thence into Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila; having shorn his head in Cenchrea: for he had a vow.
Song of Solomon 4:2
Thy teeth are like a flock of sheep that are even shorn, which came up from the washing; whereof every one bear twins, and none is barren among them.
corruption_summary: The passage is dismissed as a local custom with nothing to say, or reduced to a rule about cloth with nothing of the doctrine that grounds it.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard modern handling of 1 Corinthians 11 is to file it under first-century Corinthian custom and move on, which conveniently removes the passage's argument along with its application. Paul does not argue from local practice. He argues from the created order — the head of the woman is the man, the man is not of the woman but the woman of the man — and from the angels, and from nature itself. A reader may conclude that the covering is a cultural expression of a permanent truth, and many faithful churches have. He may not conclude that the truth expressed was also cultural, since Paul roots it in Genesis and not in Corinth.

The opposite error keeps the cloth and loses the doctrine, so that a head covering becomes a badge of party and the headship it signifies goes unpreached and unpractised in the homes of the people wearing it. Paul's concern in the chapter is order in worship and the visible acknowledgment of a real creational relation. A congregation may debate the sign; it cannot set aside what the sign is for. The complementarian order of 1 Corinthians 11:3 is the dictionary's standard, and it is exactly what both corruptions manage to avoid discussing.
roots_summary: Greek keiro (G2751), to shear or crop — 1 Corinthians 11:6, Acts 18:18; xurao (G3587), to shave with a razor — 1 Corinthians 11:5-6, Acts 21:24; Hebrew qatsab, shorn — Song of Solomon 4:2.
roots_lines: Greek keiro (G2751) — to cut the hair, to shear; 1 Corinthians 11:6, Acts 18:18, and Acts 8:32 of a lamb before its shearer.
Greek xurao (G3587) — to shave; distinguished from keiro in 1 Corinthians 11:5-6, and used of the vow in Acts 21:24.
Greek katakalupto (G2619) — to cover wholly; the verb behind covered throughout the passage.
Hebrew qatsab — shorn, cut; Song of Solomon 4:2, of the washed and shorn flock.
1 Corinthians 11:3 supplies the ground of the whole argument: the head of every man is Christ; and the head of the woman is the man; and the head of Christ is God.
usage: “If the woman be not covered, let her also be shorn” — an argument from consistency.
“Having shorn his head in Cenchrea: for he had a vow” — Paul under a Nazarite-style vow.
“A flock of sheep that are even shorn, which came up from the washing” — the image is of whiteness and order.

pos: adj. (put out, quenched; used of a man's days at the end of life and of an army snuffed out like a wick)
etymology: Latin exstinctus, past participle of exstinguere, to quench or put out. The image in both biblical uses is a flame that has gone out, not a species that has died away — the modern biological sense is later.
biblical_def: Job, at the lowest point of his complaint, says: “My breath is corrupt, my days are extinct, the graves are ready for me” (Job 17:1). The figure is a lamp burning down — the days are not stolen but spent, and the wick is out. He adds in the next breath, “Are there not mockers with me? and doth not mine eye continue in their provocation?” (Job 17:2), so the extinction he feels is aggravated by comforters who will not comfort. Isaiah uses the word of the destruction of Egypt's army at the sea: the LORD “bringeth forth the chariot and horse, the army and the power; they shall lie down together, they shall not rise: they are extinct, they are quenched as tow” (Isaiah 43:17). Quenched as tow is a striking picture — tow is the coarse fibre of flax, which flares up and is gone. The whole force of Pharaoh's chariotry is a handful of burning tow before the God who “maketh a way in the sea, and a path in the mighty waters” (Isaiah 43:16). And Isaiah's purpose in recalling it is not nostalgia: the next verse tells them to remember it no more, for He will do a new thing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines extinct as extinguished, put out, quenched, and also as having no survivor or being at an end.
webster_full: EXTINCT, a. Extinguished; put out; quenched; as, a fire, a light or a lamp is extinct.
2. Being at an end; having no survivor; as, a family or race is extinct.
3. Being at an end; having ceased.
EXTINGUISH, v.t. To put out; to quench; to suffocate; to destroy; as, to extinguish fire or flame.
TOW, n. The coarse and broken part of flax or hemp, separated from the finer part by the hatchel.
scriptures: Job 17:1
My breath is corrupt, my days are extinct, the graves are ready for me.
Isaiah 43:17
Which bringeth forth the chariot and horse, the army and the power; they shall lie down together, they shall not rise: they are extinct, they are quenched as tow.
Isaiah 43:16
Thus saith the LORD, which maketh a way in the sea, and a path in the mighty waters;
Job 17:2
Are there not mockers with me? and doth not mine eye continue in their provocation?
corruption_summary: The despair of a righteous sufferer is treated as a failure of faith to be corrected, when Scripture records it without rebuke.
corruption_paragraphs: Job 17:1 is the kind of verse that embarrasses a certain sort of piety. A righteous man says his days are burnt out and the graves are ready for him, and no narrator steps in to correct him. Scripture is willing to record the speech of a saint at the end of his resources, and the book of Job exists partly to show that the comforters, who had a tidy explanation for everything, were the ones God rebuked. A church that permits no such speech, and treats every expression of anguish as unbelief to be talked out of, has adopted the theology of Eliphaz while quoting the words of Job. The Psalms are full of the same register, and the darkest of them ends without resolution.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what Isaiah does with the word. He recalls the greatest deliverance in the nation's history — the chariots quenched as tow — and then tells them to remember it no more, because God is about to do a new thing. Memory of past mercy is not the goal; it is the ground for expecting present mercy. Congregations that live entirely on the recollection of a former season, and congregations that despise the past altogether, have each taken half of Isaiah 43 and left the half that corrects them.
roots_summary: Hebrew zaak, to be extinguished — Job 17:1; daak, to go out or be quenched — Isaiah 43:17; neoreth, tow — Isaiah 43:17.
roots_lines: Hebrew zaak — to be extinguished, snuffed out; Job 17:1, of a man's days.
Hebrew daak — to go out, be quenched; Isaiah 43:17, and Proverbs 13:9 of the lamp of the wicked.
Hebrew neoreth — tow, the coarse fibre of flax; Isaiah 43:17, and Judges 16:9 of the cords Samson snapped.
Hebrew qeber — a grave; Job 17:1, in the plural, the graves are ready for me.
Isaiah 43:18-19 supplies the turn: remember ye not the former things, for behold, I will do a new thing.
usage: “My days are extinct, the graves are ready for me” — recorded without rebuke.
“They are extinct, they are quenched as tow” — Pharaoh's chariots as burning flax.
The figure is a wick gone out, not a species died away.
